books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin, vol. 1 (1852)

stimulus.source_note: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly, vol. 1, title page (Boston: John P. Jewett & Company, 1852). Public domain.
stimulus.text: The title page of the first book edition of Uncle Tom's Cabin, published in Boston in 1852, reads “UNCLE TOM'S CABIN; OR, LIFE AMONG THE LOWLY. BY HARRIET BEECHER STOWE.” Below the title, an engraving shows a woman standing in the doorway of a log cabin, with children and a man carrying an axe nearby. The page also states “VOL. I.” and “TENTH THOUSAND,” meaning ten thousand copies had already been printed.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: What does the title page itself show about Uncle Tom's Cabin's early sales?

options.text: It was selling fast: the page marks this copy “TENTH THOUSAND.”
It had sold more than a million copies before publication.
options.misconception: The page itself claims only the tenth thousand; a million copies is not on this page.

options.text: It was printed only in Boston and Cleveland.
options.misconception: Boston and Cleveland are the publishers' cities, not the only places the book sold; the page names the publishers, not the sales territory.

options.text: It was published as a single volume in 1851.
options.misconception: The page says “VOL. I.” — volume one — and gives the year 1852, not 1851.

rationales.A: The page states “TENTH THOUSAND,” meaning ten thousand copies had already been printed by the time this copy was made.
rationales.B: The page itself claims only the tenth thousand; a million copies is not on this page.
rationales.C: Boston and Cleveland are the publishers' cities, not the only places the book sold; the page names the publishers, not the sales territory.
rationales.D: The page says “VOL. I.” — volume one — and gives the year 1852, not 1851.
rationales.general:
1. Look past the title to the small print at the bottom of the page.
2. Read what it says: “TENTH THOUSAND” — ten thousand copies already printed.
3. Ask what that number means for a new book: readers were buying it faster than the press could keep up.
Remember: a book's title page can be evidence too; print numbers tell you how fast it sold.
